{{Short description|Nonabelian cryptographic protocol}}
'''Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld protocol''', also known as a '''commutator key exchange''', is a key-exchange protocol using [[nonabelian group]]s. It was invented by Drs. Michael Anshel, Iris Anshel, and [[Dorian M. Goldfeld|Dorian Goldfeld]]. Unlike other group-based protocols, it does not employ any commuting or commutative subgroups of a given platform group and can use any nonabelian group with efficiently computable normal forms. It is often discussed specifically in application of [[braid groups]], which notably are infinite (and the group elements can take variable quantities of space to represent). The computed [[shared secret]] is an element of the group, so in practice this scheme must be accompanied with a sufficiently secure compressive [[hash function]] to normalize the group element to a usable bitstring.

== Description ==
Let <math>G</math> be a fixed nonabelian [[Group (mathematics)|group]] called a ''platform group''.

'''Alice's public/private information:'''

* ''Alice's public key'' is a [[tuple]] of elements <math>{\bf a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)</math> in <math>G</math>. 
* ''Alice's private key'' is a sequence of elements from <math>{\bf a}</math> and their inverses: <math>a_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}, \ldots, a_{i_L}^{\varepsilon_L}</math>, where <math>a_{i_k}\in{\bf a}</math> and <math>\varepsilon_k=\pm 1</math>. Based on that sequence she computes the product <math>A = a_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1} \ldots a_{i_L}^{\varepsilon_L}</math>.

'''Bob's public/private information:'''

* ''Bob's public key'' is a tuple of elements <math>{\bf b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)</math> in <math>G</math>. 
* ''Bob's private key'' is a sequence of elements from <math>{\bf b}</math> and their inverses: <math>b_{j_1}^{\delta_1}, \ldots, b_{j_L}^{\delta_L}</math>, where <math>b_{j_k}\in{\bf b}</math> and <math>\delta_k=\pm 1</math>. Based on that sequence he computes the product <math>B = b_{j_1}^{\delta_1} \ldots b_{j_L}^{\delta_L}</math>.

'''Transitions:'''

* Alice sends a tuple <math>{\overline{\bf a}}=(A^{-1}b_1A,\ldots,A^{-1}b_nA)</math> to Bob.
* Bob sends a tuple <math>{\overline{\bf b}}=(B^{-1}a_1B,\ldots,B^{-1}a_nB)</math> to Alice.

'''Shared key:'''

The key shared by [[Alice and Bob]] is the group element <math>K = A^{-1} B^{-1} A B \in G</math> called the [[commutator]] of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>.

* Alice computes <math>K</math> as a product <math>A^{-1} \cdot \left(B^{-1}a_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}B\right)\cdots \left(B^{-1}a_{i_L}^{\varepsilon_L}B\right) = A^{-1} B^{-1} A B</math>.
* Bob computes <math>K</math> as a product <math>\left(A^{-1}b_{j_L}^{-\delta_L}A\right) \cdots \left(A^{-1} b_{j_1}^{-\delta_1}A^{}\right) \cdot B = A^{-1} B^{-1} A B</math>.

==Security==
From the standpoint of an attacker trying to attack the protocol, they usually learn the public keys <math>\bf a</math> and <math>\bf b</math>, and the conjugated public keys <math>\overline{\bf a}</math> and <math>\overline{\bf b}</math>. A direct attack then consists of trying to find a suitable <math>A</math> that is generated by the elements of <math>\bf a</math>, and that produces the appropriate conjugations <math>\overline{\bf a}</math> when applied. (An 'indirect' attack would consist of trying to find <math>K</math> directly, which would require some additional special structure of the group.) For this reason the public keys <math>\bf a</math> and <math>\bf b</math> must be chosen to generate a large subgroup of <math>G</math> — ideally, they form a full set of generators, so that <math>A</math> cannot be constrained just by knowing that is generated from <math>\bf a</math>.

Solving for a suitable <math>A</math> given the conjugation relations is called the ''conjugation problem'', and substantial research has been done on attacks to the [[conjugacy problem]] on [[braid group]]s, although no full efficient solution has achieved.
